parameter: Effect of monetary policy on house prices
headline: a 1.2% fall in house prices per 1-percentage-point policy rate rise, peaking after two years
caveat: correcting for publication bias alone gives 0.23%, but conditioning on best practice offsets it
basis: 1,555 estimates from 237 impulse responses in 37 studies
source: Ehrenbergerova et al. 2023, IMF Economic Review
sentence: Effect of monetary policy on house prices: corrected for publication bias and misspecification, a 1.2% fall in house prices per 1-percentage-point policy rate rise, peaking after two years (correcting for publication bias alone gives 0.23%, but conditioning on best practice offsets it), based on 1,555 estimates from 237 impulse responses in 37 studies (Ehrenbergerova et al. 2023, IMF Economic Review).
source_quote: As the bottom line of our analysis we compute the impulse response implied by the entire literature but conditional on the absence of publication bias and potential misspecifications. ... The mean maximum corrected semi-elasticity is -1.2 ... Our results suggest that a one-percentage-point increase in the policy rate is on average associated with a maximum decrease of 1.2% in house prices after two years.

parameter: Effect of structural reforms on economic growth
headline: reforms in transition countries cost growth in the short run but raise it strongly in the long run, and that holds after correcting for publication bias
source: Babecky and Havranek 2014, Economics of Transition
sentence: Effect of structural reforms on economic growth: reforms in transition countries cost growth in the short run but raise it strongly in the long run, and that holds after correcting for publication bias, based on 60 studies with 537 estimates (Babecky and Havranek 2014, Economics of Transition).
source_quote: Our results show that an average reform caused substantial costs in the short run, but had strong positive effects on long-run growth. ... The findings hold even after correction for publication bias and misspecifications present in some primary studies. ... In total, 60 studies issued since 1996 are included ... they contain 537 empirical estimates

parameter: Elasticity of intertemporal substitution in consumption
caveat: micro estimates for asset holders; macro mean zero
source: Havranek 2015, Journal of the European Economic Association
sentence: Elasticity of intertemporal substitution in consumption: corrected for publication bias, 0.3-0.4 (micro estimates for asset holders; macro mean zero), based on 2,735 estimates from 169 published studies (Havranek 2015, Journal of the European Economic Association).
source_quote: The corrected mean of micro estimates of the EIS for asset holders is around 0.3-0.4.

parameter: Elasticity of substitution between capital and labor
caveat: best-practice specification; the mean reported estimate is 0.9
source: Gechert et al. 2022, Review of Economic Dynamics
sentence: Elasticity of substitution between capital and labor: the meta-analytic estimate is 0.3 (best-practice specification; the mean reported estimate is 0.9), based on 3,186 estimates from 121 studies (Gechert et al. 2022, Review of Economic Dynamics).
source_quote: The mean elasticity conditional on the absence of publication bias, disaggregated data, and inclusion of information from the first-order condition for capital is 0.3.

parameter: Excess sensitivity of consumption to anticipated income changes
headline: 0.11, against a mean reported estimate of 0.37
source: Havranek and Sokolova 2020, Review of Economic Dynamics
sentence: Excess sensitivity of consumption to anticipated income changes: the estimate corrected for aggregation and publication bias is 0.11, against a mean reported estimate of 0.37, based on about 3,000 estimates from 144 studies (Havranek and Sokolova 2020, Review of Economic Dynamics).
source_quote: When corrected for the bias due to aggregation and the bias due to publication selection, the literature yields a mean excess sensitivity of merely 0.11.

parameter: Optimal long-run inflation rate
headline: about 0.6% per year
caveat: calibration-dominated model literature
source: Opatrny et al. 2026
sentence: Optimal long-run inflation rate: the meta-analytic estimate is about 0.6% per year (calibration-dominated model literature), based on 777 estimates from 116 primary studies (Opatrny et al. 2026).
source_quote: Across publication-selection and selection-on-significance diagnostics that are applicable in this calibration-dominated corpus, the literature points to an optimum of roughly 0.6 percentage points per year, well below the two-percent targets commonly used by advanced-economy central banks.

parameter: The price puzzle (prices rising after monetary tightening)
headline: it disappears once publication and misspecification biases are corrected, and prices fall instead, bottoming out 0.33% below baseline six months after a 1-percentage-point rate rise
source: Rusnak et al. 2013, Journal of Money, Credit and Banking
sentence: The price puzzle (prices rising after monetary tightening): it disappears once publication and misspecification biases are corrected, and prices fall instead, bottoming out 0.33% below baseline six months after a 1-percentage-point rate rise, based on about 1,000 estimates from 70 studies (Rusnak et al. 2013, Journal of Money, Credit and Banking).
source_quote: After controlling for both publication and misspecification biases, the price puzzle is not present and prices bottom out 6 months after a 1 percentage point increase in the interest rate. The maximum decrease in the price level reaches 0.33% and is statistically significant at the 5% level.

parameter: Transmission lag of monetary policy to prices
headline: 29 months on average, but 25-50 months in developed economies against 10-20 in post-transition ones; the factor explaining that gap is financial development, with greater development meaning slower transmission
caveat: prices bottom out 0.9% below baseline after a 1-percentage-point hike
source: Havranek and Rusnak 2013, International Journal of Central Banking
sentence: Transmission lag of monetary policy to prices: the meta-analytic estimate is 29 months on average, but 25-50 months in developed economies against 10-20 in post-transition ones; the factor explaining that gap is financial development, with greater development meaning slower transmission (prices bottom out 0.9% below baseline after a 1-percentage-point hike), based on 67 published studies (Havranek and Rusnak 2013, International Journal of Central Banking).
source_quote: The average transmission lag is twenty-nine months, and the maximum decrease in prices reaches 0.9 percent on average after a 1-percentage-point hike in the policy rate. Transmission lags are longer in developed economies (twenty-five to fifty months) than in post-transition economies (ten to twenty months). We find that the factor most effective in explaining this heterogeneity is financial development: greater financial development is associated with slower transmission.

parameter: Why intertemporal substitution varies across countries
headline: income and asset market participation explain most of the cross-country heterogeneity
basis: 2,735 estimates from 169 published studies covering 104 countries
source: Havranek et al. 2015, Journal of International Economics
sentence: Why intertemporal substitution varies across countries: the meta-analytic finding is income and asset market participation explain most of the cross-country heterogeneity, based on 2,735 estimates from 169 published studies covering 104 countries (Havranek et al. 2015, Journal of International Economics).
source_quote: income and asset market participation are the most effective factors in explaining the heterogeneity

parameter: Beauty premium in earnings
headline: 1.1% (95% CrI -0.8% to 3.0%)
caveat: controlling for cognitive ability; large only for sex workers
source: Irsova et al. 2025
sentence: Beauty premium in earnings: the meta-analytic estimate is 1.1% (95% CrI -0.8% to 3.0%; controlling for cognitive ability; large only for sex workers), based on 1,159 estimates in 67 studies (Irsova et al. 2025).
source_quote: Second, controlling for cognitive ability renders the premium small (mean = 1.1%; 95% CrI = -0.8%, 3.0%) for all occupations except sex workers, where appearance is a direct input.

parameter: Coefficient of relative risk aversion
headline: 1 in economics, 2-7 in finance
caveat: from consumption Euler equation studies
source: Elminejad et al. 2025, Journal of Economic Surveys
sentence: Coefficient of relative risk aversion: corrected for publication bias, 1 in economics, 2-7 in finance (from consumption Euler equation studies), based on 1,021 estimates from 92 studies (Elminejad et al. 2025, Journal of Economic Surveys).
source_quote: After correction for the bias, the literature suggests a mean risk aversion of 1 in economics and 2-7 in finance contexts.

parameter: Effect of financial incentives on performance
headline: about 0
caveat: field contexts; lab and loss framing modestly positive
source: Cala et al. 2026, Journal of Political Economy Microeconomics, forthcoming
sentence: Effect of financial incentives on performance: corrected for publication bias, about 0 (field contexts; lab and loss framing modestly positive), based on 2,193 estimates from 88 economics experiments (Cala et al. 2026, Journal of Political Economy Microeconomics, forthcoming).
source_quote: Using recent advances in correcting for publication bias and p-hacking, we find that the corrected mean effect of financial incentives on performance is close to zero across most field contexts.

parameter: Effect of physical exercise on cognition
headline: SMD 0.227 for general cognition, 0.027 for memory and 0.012 for executive function
caveat: wide prediction intervals spanning negative and positive effects
source: Bartoš et al. 2025
sentence: Effect of physical exercise on cognition: corrected for publication bias, SMD 0.227 for general cognition, 0.027 for memory and 0.012 for executive function (wide prediction intervals spanning negative and positive effects), based on 2,239 effect-size estimates from 215 meta-analyses (Bartoš et al. 2025).
source_quote: Analyses adjusted for publication bias reveal average effects much smaller than commonly reported (general cognition: standardized mean difference, SMD = 0.227, 95% credible interval 0.116 to 0.330; memory: SMD = 0.027, 95% credible interval 0.000 to 0.227; executive functions: SMD = 0.012, 95% credible interval 0.000 to 0.147), along with wide prediction intervals spanning both negative and positive effects.

parameter: Habit formation in consumption
headline: 0.4 (macro 0.6, micro 0.1)
caveat: mean reported estimate, with no correction for publication bias
source: Havranek et al. 2017, European Economic Review
sentence: Habit formation in consumption: the meta-analytic estimate is 0.4 (macro 0.6, micro 0.1; mean reported estimate, with no correction for publication bias), based on 597 estimates from 81 published studies (Havranek et al. 2017, European Economic Review).
source_quote: The mean reported strength of habit formation equals 0.4, but the estimates vary widely both within and across studies. We use Bayesian and frequentist model averaging to assign a pattern to this variance while taking into account model uncertainty. Studies employing macro data report consistently larger estimates than micro studies: 0.6 vs. 0.1 on average.

parameter: Individual discount rate (impatience measured in experiments)
headline: 33% per year
source: Matousek et al. 2022, Experimental Economics
sentence: Individual discount rate (impatience measured in experiments): corrected for publication bias, 33% per year, based on 927 estimates from 56 studies (Matousek et al. 2022, Experimental Economics).
source_quote: The corrected mean annual discount rate is 0.33.

parameter: Climate sensitivity (warming from a doubling of CO2)
headline: 1.4-2.3 degrees Celsius
caveat: historical-record estimate; the IPCC AR6 assessment is about 3 C
source: Reckova and Irsova 2015, Energy and Environment
sentence: Climate sensitivity (warming from a doubling of CO2): corrected for publication bias, 1.4-2.3 degrees Celsius (historical-record estimate; the IPCC AR6 assessment is about 3 C), based on 48 estimates from 16 studies (Reckova and Irsova 2015, Energy and Environment).
source_quote: Corrected for publication bias, the bulk of the literature is consistent with climate sensitivity lying between 1.4 and 2.3 degrees Celsius.

parameter: Electricity savings from daylight saving time
headline: essentially zero, 0.01% savings, against a 0.34% simple average of reported estimates
caveat: savings during the days DST applies; the paper finds no publication bias in this literature, so this is a methodological correction
source: Havranek et al. 2018, Energy Journal
sentence: Electricity savings from daylight saving time: the best-practice estimate is essentially zero, 0.01% savings, against a 0.34% simple average of reported estimates (savings during the days DST applies; the paper finds no publication bias in this literature, so this is a methodological correction), based on 162 estimates from 44 studies (Havranek et al. 2018, Energy Journal).
source_quote: The resulting global estimate is -0.01%, quite distant from -0.34%, the simple average effect reported in the literature. ... We conclude that electricity savings from DST are, on average, negligible and highly unlikely to exceed 0.76% of total electricity consumption during the days when the daylight saving policy is in place.

parameter: Income elasticity of gasoline demand
headline: 0.1 short run, 0.23 long run
source: Havranek and Kokes 2015, Energy Economics
sentence: Income elasticity of gasoline demand: corrected for publication bias, 0.1 short run, 0.23 long run (Havranek and Kokes 2015, Energy Economics).
source_quote: Our results suggest that the income elasticity of gasoline demand is on average much smaller than reported in previous surveys: the mean corrected for publication bias is 0.1 for the short run and 0.23 for the long run.

parameter: Income elasticity of water demand
headline: about 0.15 or less
source: Havranek et al. 2018, Land Economics
sentence: Income elasticity of water demand: corrected for publication bias, about 0.15 or less, based on 307 estimates (Havranek et al. 2018, Land Economics).
source_quote: Attempting to correct simultaneously for publication and endogeneity biases, we find that the mean underlying elasticity is approximately 0.15 or less.

parameter: Natural resource curse (effect of resource richness on long-run growth)
headline: weak support for a curse
source: Havranek et al. 2016, World Development
sentence: Natural resource curse (effect of resource richness on long-run growth): the meta-analytic finding is weak support for a curse, based on 605 estimates from 43 studies (Havranek et al. 2016, World Development).
source_quote: In a quantitative survey of 605 estimates reported in 43 studies, we find that overall support for the resource curse hypothesis is weak when potential publication bias and method heterogeneity are taken into account.

parameter: Price elasticity of electricity demand
headline: -0.16 short run, -0.38 long run
caveat: best-identified short-run estimates statistically indistinguishable from zero
source: Kudela et al. 2026
sentence: Price elasticity of electricity demand: corrected for publication bias, -0.16 short run, -0.38 long run (best-identified short-run estimates statistically indistinguishable from zero), based on 4,720 estimates from 462 studies (Kudela et al. 2026).
source_quote: First, the best-identified studies find smaller responses than naive ones: the publication-bias-corrected short-run elasticity is about −0.16 (a 10% rise in the electricity price cuts consumption by under 2%), and only −0.09 among the best-identified studies, whose adjusted value is statistically indistinguishable from zero. Second, responsiveness grows with time to adjust, roughly doubling from −0.16 in the short run to −0.38 in the long run as the capital stock turns over, but this pattern has itself been stable for decades.

parameter: Price elasticity of gasoline demand
headline: -0.09 short run, -0.31 long run
source: Havranek et al. 2012, Energy Economics
sentence: Price elasticity of gasoline demand: corrected for publication bias, -0.09 short run, -0.31 long run (Havranek et al. 2012, Energy Economics).
source_quote: Using mixed-effects multilevel meta-regression, we show that after correction for publication bias the average long-run elasticity reaches -0.31 and the average short-run elasticity only -0.09.

parameter: Social cost of carbon
headline: 0-134 USD per metric ton of carbon
caveat: 2010 prices, emission year 2015; per ton of carbon, not CO2
source: Havranek et al. 2015, Energy Economics
sentence: Social cost of carbon: corrected for publication bias, 0-134 USD per metric ton of carbon (2010 prices, emission year 2015; per ton of carbon, not CO2), based on 809 estimates from 101 studies (Havranek et al. 2015, Energy Economics).
source_quote: Our estimates of the mean reported SCC corrected for the selective reporting bias range between 0 and 134 USD per ton of carbon in 2010 prices for emission year 2015.

parameter: Armington elasticity (substitution between domestic and foreign goods)
headline: 2.5-5.1, median 3.8
source: Bajzik et al. 2020, Journal of International Economics
sentence: Armington elasticity (substitution between domestic and foreign goods): the meta-analytic estimate is 2.5-5.1, median 3.8, based on 3,524 estimates (Bajzik et al. 2020, Journal of International Economics).
source_quote: Third, the elasticity implied by the literature after accounting for both publication bias and study quality lies in the range 2.5--5.1 with a median of 3.8.

parameter: Border effect on international trade
headline: one-third reduction in trade
source: Havranek and Irsova 2017, IMF Economic Review
sentence: Border effect on international trade: the meta-analytic finding is one-third reduction in trade, based on 1,271 estimates from 61 studies (Havranek and Irsova 2017, IMF Economic Review).
source_quote: We show that major methodological innovations of the last decade combine to shrink the border effect to a one-third reduction in international trade flows worldwide.

parameter: Determinants of horizontal FDI spillovers
headline: spillovers are zero on average but depend systematically on the technology gap and ownership structure; encouraging joint ventures with investors holding a smaller technology edge raises the average spillover by about 0.3
source: Irsova and Havranek 2013, World Development
sentence: Determinants of horizontal FDI spillovers: the main result is that spillovers are zero on average but depend systematically on the technology gap and ownership structure; encouraging joint ventures with investors holding a smaller technology edge raises the average spillover by about 0.3, based on 1,205 estimates screened against 43 candidate determinants (Irsova and Havranek 2013, World Development).
source_quote: Our results suggest that horizontal spillovers are on average zero, but that their sign and magnitude depend systematically on the characteristics of the domestic economy and foreign investors. The most important determinants are the technology gap between domestic and foreign firms and the ownership structure in investment projects. ... it may increase the average spillovers by 0.144 + 0.158 = 0.302, an economically significant value.

parameter: Effect of the euro on trade
headline: no detectable effect once publication bias is corrected, while other currency unions raise trade by more than 60%
source: Havranek 2010, Review of World Economics
sentence: Effect of the euro on trade: no detectable effect once publication bias is corrected, while other currency unions raise trade by more than 60% (Havranek 2010, Review of World Economics).
source_quote: However, according to the meta-regression analysis, the euro's trade promoting effect corrected for publication bias is insignificant.

parameter: FDI spillovers to domestic firm productivity (Czech Republic)
headline: +11% productivity per 10-percentage-point rise in foreign presence
caveat: as of 2018; 19% for joint ventures
source: Hampl et al. 2020, Applied Economics
sentence: FDI spillovers to domestic firm productivity (Czech Republic): the meta-analytic estimate is +11% productivity per 10-percentage-point rise in foreign presence (as of 2018; 19% for joint ventures), based on 332 estimates (Hampl et al. 2020, Applied Economics).
source_quote: When placing more weight on estimates that solve important identification problems in the literature (such as using data on existing linkages between firms instead of approximations based on input-output tables), we find that, as of 2018, a 10-percentage-point increase in foreign presence is likely to lift the productivity of domestic firms by 11%.

parameter: Forward premium puzzle (slope from regressions of spot on forward rates)
headline: 0.23-0.45 for developed and 0.95-1.16 for emerging currencies
caveat: unbiasedness hypothesis predicts slope of 1
source: Zigraiova et al. 2021, European Economic Review
sentence: Forward premium puzzle (slope from regressions of spot on forward rates): corrected for publication bias, 0.23-0.45 for developed and 0.95-1.16 for emerging currencies (unbiasedness hypothesis predicts slope of 1), based on 3,643 estimates from 91 studies (Zigraiova et al. 2021, European Economic Review).
source_quote: Correcting for these biases yields slope coefficients in the intervals (0.23,0.45) and (0.95,1.16) for the currencies of developed and emerging countries respectively.

parameter: Vertical FDI spillovers to suppliers and buyers
headline: about 9% higher productivity for suppliers per 10-percentage-point rise in foreign presence, small for buyers and none within the sector
source: Havranek and Irsova 2011, Journal of International Economics
sentence: Vertical FDI spillovers to suppliers and buyers: the estimate corrected for publication and misspecification bias is about 9% higher productivity for suppliers per 10-percentage-point rise in foreign presence, small for buyers and none within the sector, based on 3,626 estimates (Havranek and Irsova 2011, Journal of International Economics).
source_quote: Taking into consideration publication and misspecification bias, our preferred estimate suggests that a 10-percentage-point increase in foreign presence is associated with an increase in the productivity of domestic firms in supplier sectors of about 9%.

parameter: Effect of class size on student achievement
headline: about 0
caveat: except in the STAR experiment and classes under 15 students
source: Opatrny et al. 2025, Journal of Labor Economics
sentence: Effect of class size on student achievement: the meta-analytic estimate is about 0 (except in the STAR experiment and classes under 15 students), based on 2,819 estimates from 66 studies (Opatrny et al. 2025, Journal of Labor Economics).
source_quote: The implied class size effect is negligible for all identification approaches except Tennessee's Student/Teacher Achievement Ratio project and for all contexts except classes of fewer than 15 students.

parameter: Effect of working while in school on educational outcomes
headline: about 0, slightly negative
caveat: more substantive for dropout decisions
source: Kroupova et al. 2024, Economics of Education Review
sentence: Effect of working while in school on educational outcomes: the meta-analytic estimate is about 0, slightly negative (more substantive for dropout decisions), based on 861 estimates from 69 studies (Kroupova et al. 2024, Economics of Education Review).
source_quote: Overall the literature suggests a negative but economically inconsequential mean effect.

parameter: Elasticity of substitution between native and immigrant workers
headline: about 17
caveat: baseline regional specification; simple bias correction implies 22
source: Kantova et al. 2026
sentence: Elasticity of substitution between native and immigrant workers: corrected for publication bias, about 17 (baseline regional specification; simple bias correction implies 22), based on 1,091 estimates from 41 studies (Kantova et al. 2026).
source_quote: Our best-practice estimates, which net out publication bias and prioritize the most granular data, imply an elasticity of about 17 in our baseline regional specification, lower than implied by a simple bias correction but substantially higher than the uncorrected mean.

parameter: Elasticity of substitution between skilled and unskilled labor
headline: 4, with a lower bound of 2 and smaller values in developing countries
source: Havranek et al. 2024, Review of Economics and Statistics
sentence: Elasticity of substitution between skilled and unskilled labor: the meta-analytic estimate is 4, with a lower bound of 2 and smaller values in developing countries, based on 682 estimates from 77 studies (Havranek et al. 2024, Review of Economics and Statistics).
source_quote: The implied mean elasticity is 4, with a lower bound of 2.

parameter: Frisch elasticity of labor supply (intertemporal substitution in hours worked)
headline: about 0.25 for total hours
caveat: 0.2 on the intensive margin, near zero on the extensive
source: Elminejad et al. 2023, Review of Economic Dynamics
sentence: Frisch elasticity of labor supply (intertemporal substitution in hours worked): the meta-analytic estimate is about 0.25 for total hours (0.2 on the intensive margin, near zero on the extensive), based on over 700 estimates for each margin (Elminejad et al. 2023, Review of Economic Dynamics).
source_quote: A total hours elasticity of about 0.25 is the most consistent with empirical evidence.

parameter: Learning loss from COVID-19 school closures
headline: about -0.12 SD, roughly 30% of a school year
source: Luskova et al. 2026
sentence: Learning loss from COVID-19 school closures: the meta-analytic estimate is about -0.12 SD, roughly 30% of a school year (Luskova et al. 2026).
source_quote: Our preferred specifications, RoBMA and MAIVE, rely on different assumptions yet converge on an effect size of approximately −0.12 SD, equivalent to a learning loss of about 30% of a school year.

parameter: Tuition-enrollment elasticity (effect of tuition on university enrollment)
headline: about 0
source: Havranek et al. 2018, Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics
sentence: Tuition-enrollment elasticity (effect of tuition on university enrollment): corrected for publication bias, about 0, based on 443 estimates from 43 studies (Havranek et al. 2018, Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics).
source_quote: After correcting for this publication bias, we find that the literature is consistent with the mean tuition-enrollment elasticity being close to zero.

parameter: Effect of bank competition on financial stability
headline: about 0
source: Zigraiova and Havranek 2016, Journal of Economic Surveys
sentence: Effect of bank competition on financial stability: corrected for publication bias, about 0, based on 598 estimates from 31 studies (Zigraiova and Havranek 2016, Journal of Economic Surveys).
source_quote: Taken together, the estimates reported in the literature suggest little interplay between competition and stability, even when corrected for publication bias and potential misspecifications.

parameter: Effect of board gender diversity on ESG performance
headline: about 0.12 ESG points per 1-pp diversity increase
caveat: higher in the Middle East, about zero in Southeast Asia
source: Hozova et al. 2026
sentence: Effect of board gender diversity on ESG performance: the meta-analytic estimate is about 0.12 ESG points per 1-pp diversity increase (higher in the Middle East, about zero in Southeast Asia), based on 533 estimates from 106 studies (Hozova et al. 2026).
source_quote: A best-practice estimate that also imposes sound study design puts it near 0.12 for most of the world, markedly higher for the Middle East, and essentially zero, if anything slightly negative, for the Southeast Asian markets that dominate the Asian evidence.

parameter: Effect of financial development on economic growth
headline: positive but widely varying; studies ignoring endogeneity overstate it, and the effect weakens after the 1980s and in poorer countries
source: Valickova et al. 2015, Journal of Economic Surveys
sentence: Effect of financial development on economic growth: the meta-analytic estimate is positive but widely varying; studies ignoring endogeneity overstate it, and the effect weakens after the 1980s and in poorer countries, based on 1,334 estimates from 67 studies (Valickova et al. 2015, Journal of Economic Surveys).
source_quote: Taken together, the studies imply a positive and statistically significant effect, but the individual estimates vary widely.

parameter: Effect of remittances on economic growth
headline: positive but economically small
caveat: growth-enhancing in Asia but not Africa
source: Cazachevici et al. 2020, World Development
sentence: Effect of remittances on economic growth: the meta-analytic finding is positive but economically small (growth-enhancing in Asia but not Africa), based on 538 estimates from 95 studies (Cazachevici et al. 2020, World Development).
source_quote: Correcting for the bias using recently developed techniques, we find that the mean effect of remittances on growth is still positive but economically small.

parameter: Hedge fund alpha (monthly risk-adjusted return)
headline: 30-40 basis points per month
caveat: gross of fees; the companion study finds about zero after fees and design
source: Yang et al. 2024, Journal of Economic Surveys
sentence: Hedge fund alpha (monthly risk-adjusted return): corrected for publication bias, 30-40 basis points per month (gross of fees; the companion study finds about zero after fees and design), based on 1,019 alpha estimates from 74 studies (Yang et al. 2024, Journal of Economic Surveys).
source_quote: Most of our monthly alpha estimates adjusted for the (small) bias fall within a relatively narrow range of 30 to 40 basis points.

parameter: Size premium in stock returns
headline: 1.72% per year
caveat: smallest vs. largest capitalization quintile
source: Astakhov et al. 2019, Journal of Economic Surveys
sentence: Size premium in stock returns: corrected for publication bias, 1.72% per year (smallest vs. largest capitalization quintile), based on 1,746 estimates from 102 published studies (Astakhov et al. 2019, Journal of Economic Surveys).
source_quote: After correcting for the bias, we find that the literature suggests a size premium (the difference in annual stock returns on the smallest and largest capitalization quintile) of 1.72%.

parameter: Stock-price reaction to shareholder activism
headline: 0% to 1.5%
source: Bajzik et al. 2025, Corporate Governance: An International Review
sentence: Stock-price reaction to shareholder activism: corrected for publication bias, 0% to 1.5%, based on 1,973 estimates from 67 studies (Bajzik et al. 2025, Corporate Governance: An International Review).
source_quote: Corrected activism effects range from 0% to 1.5%.

parameter: Trust, rule of law, and the size premium in stock returns
headline: stronger rule of law, larger size premium
caveat: association in reported estimates, not causal
source: Schwarz et al. 2026
sentence: Trust, rule of law, and the size premium in stock returns: the meta-analytic finding is stronger rule of law, larger size premium (association in reported estimates, not causal), based on 1,613 estimates from 105 studies and 31 countries (Schwarz et al. 2026).
source_quote: The more stable association is with rule of law, and it runs against the intuitive expectation that better legal institutions shrink the premium: stronger rule of law is associated with more negative reported size slopes, hence larger conventional size premia.

parameter: Variation in hedge fund alphas
headline: 9 of 34 study characteristics consistently explain it, above all whether alpha is measured gross or net of fees, a gap of 0.439 percentage points a month; expected alphas under best practice are close to zero for all common strategies
source: Yang et al. 2026
sentence: Variation in hedge fund alphas: the main result is that 9 of 34 study characteristics consistently explain it, above all whether alpha is measured gross or net of fees, a gap of 0.439 percentage points a month; expected alphas under best practice are close to zero for all common strategies, based on 1,019 estimates from 74 studies (Yang et al. 2026).
source_quote: We document that 9 out of the 34 characteristics we analyze are consistently relevant to explain the variation in the reported estimates. ... when considering the fees and the variation in research designs, the current estimates of expected alphas implied by the best practice methodology are close to zero for all common hedge fund strategies.

parameter: Bias in meta-analyses of correlations
headline: conventional fixed- and random-effects estimators are biased; the UWLS+3 and Hunter-Schmidt estimators correct this
source: Stanley et al. 2025, Research Synthesis Methods
sentence: Bias in meta-analyses of correlations: the methodological finding is that conventional fixed- and random-effects estimators are biased; the UWLS+3 and Hunter-Schmidt estimators correct this (Stanley et al. 2025, Research Synthesis Methods).
source_quote: Conventional meta-analyses (both fixed and random effects) of correlations are biased

parameter: Bias in meta-analyses of partial correlations
headline: all such meta-analyses are biased; the UWLS+3 weighted average corrects them
source: Stanley et al. 2024, Research Synthesis Methods
sentence: Bias in meta-analyses of partial correlations: the methodological finding is that all such meta-analyses are biased; the UWLS+3 weighted average corrects them (Stanley et al. 2024, Research Synthesis Methods).
source_quote: We demonstrate that all meta-analyses of partial correlations are biased

parameter: How to run a modern meta-analysis
headline: a concise, nontechnical, step-by-step guide for practitioners, treating publication bias, p-hacking and heterogeneity as problems every meta-analyst must confront
source: Irsova et al. 2024, Journal of Economic Surveys
sentence: How to run a modern meta-analysis: a concise, nontechnical, step-by-step guide for practitioners, treating publication bias, p-hacking and heterogeneity as problems every meta-analyst must confront (Irsova et al. 2024, Journal of Economic Surveys).
source_quote: This paper provides concise, nontechnical, step-by-step guidelines on how to conduct a modern meta-analysis

parameter: Sensitivity of meta-analysis results to outlier handling
headline: median shift at most 0.047 (Cohen's d); significance flips in 11.5% of cases
caveat: across four pre-registered outlier treatments and two estimators
source: Havranek et al. 2026
sentence: Sensitivity of meta-analysis results to outlier handling: the methodological finding is median shift at most 0.047 (Cohen's d); significance flips in 11.5% of cases (across four pre-registered outlier treatments and two estimators), based on 358 behavioral science meta-analyses (Havranek et al. 2026).
source_quote: Alternative outlier handling treatments have little effect on the meta-analysis mean as the median absolute change in Cohen's d is at most 0.047 and often much less. Yet, at least one of these four treatments in combination with one of these estimators reverses the statistical significance of 11.5% of meta-analyses and the smallest-effect-of-interest assessment in 15.9%.

parameter: Whether the estimator choice matters for partial correlations in practice
headline: small-sample biases are negligible and Fisher's z helps with neither them nor publication selection bias; UWLS and Hunter-Schmidt give smaller, arguably less biased means than random effects
basis: 172 economics meta-analyses with 63,730 partial correlations from 6,191 papers
source: Stanley et al. 2026
sentence: Whether the estimator choice matters for partial correlations in practice: the methodological finding is that small-sample biases are negligible and Fisher's z helps with neither them nor publication selection bias; UWLS and Hunter-Schmidt give smaller, arguably less biased means than random effects, based on 172 economics meta-analyses with 63,730 partial correlations from 6,191 papers (Stanley et al. 2026).
source_quote: We find that small-sample biases are negligible in practice. However, some publication selection biases remain. Although Fisher's z transformations have often been recommended, they reduce neither small-sample nor publication selection biases relative to conventional random effects. Both the unrestricted weighted least squares (UWLS) and the Hunter-Schmidt (HS) estimators produce smaller, arguably less biased, estimates of the mean PCC in these applications than either random effects or Fisher's z transformations.
